SK2063 The operator sequence reads as a different operator

An = is written hard against a following unary -, + or ! and separated from the operand — x =- 1 — so the pair reads as the compound operator -= and is not one.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.3
SupersedesS2757

Why

x =- 1 assigns negative one. x -= 1 subtracts one. C# has no =- operator, so the compiler splits the two characters silently and the reader's eye does not. ⚠ The whitespace is the entire signal, and it is the only signal there is. x = -1 and x =- 1 are the same program and differ only in layout, so nothing semantic can separate the deliberate from the mistyped; what separates them is that somebody wrote the = and the sign as one token and then put a space before the number, which is how -= is spelled and not how a negative literal is. A rule that ignored trivia here would have nothing left to look at.

Example

Instead of:

remaining =- 1;

Write:

remaining -= 1;

// or, if assignment really was meant, written so it reads that way:
remaining = -1;

When it does not fire

⚠ Two conditions must hold together, and each one alone would over-fire. The = and the unary operator must be adjacent with no trivia between them, and the unary operator must be separated from its operand by trivia. x = -1 and x = - 1 fail the first; x =-1 and x=-1 fail the second, and they are how a negative literal gets written in a hurry and in a compressed style. Only the asymmetric spelling — where the spacing groups the two operator characters together and pushes the operand away — is reported, whether or not there is a space before the =. ⚠ A third condition, "there is space before the `=`", was in the first draft and was removed because a sabotage could not reach it: no fixture separated it from the other two, and x=- 1 groups and pushes exactly as x =- 1 does, so declining it was an exemption with no argument behind it. ⚠ The rule reads the trivia of the tree as parsed, which is the source as the author wrote it; it draws no conclusion from what the formatter would produce, and running the formatter over the file is one of the ways to make the finding go away. Only -, + and ! are considered: they are the unary operators whose characters also start a compound assignment (-=, +=, !=). A ~ or a & has no such reading. Compound assignments themselves are not examined, and neither is any binary operator, and neither is a variable declarator's =, which is not an assignment expression. ⚠ There is no fix, deliberately: x -= 1 and x = -1 are both plausible readings and they are different programs, so an automatic repair would have to guess which bug it was looking at. ⚠ Measured on the 4 459-file corpus, and the second condition is what earned its place there. The shipped rule reports nothing. Widened to look only at the =/sign adjacency, it reports 17 occurrences, every one of them inside Testing/corpus/unformatted/collapse/ — a slice whose whole purpose is to strip whitespace, so GoalIndex = -1; is stored as GoalIndex=-1;. The operand is not pushed away from the sign in any of them, which is why the rule declines all 17. A tool that reads whitespace for meaning meets machine-mangled whitespace sooner than most, and this is what that looks like. Generated code is excluded.
